newsitem.title: GERMANY: German IBIS DAX index ends stable at lower levels.
newsitem.headline: German IBIS DAX index ends stable at lower levels.

text.p: Germany's IBIS DAX index ended trade on Thursday slightly lower but stable and off earlier lows, as a slightly lower dollar and a lower opening on Wall Street hit sentiment in German share trade.
The IBIS DAX index ended at 3,197.09 points, down 11.95 or 0.37 percent, having fallen to 3,175.21 points earlier.

Earlier the DAX index extended a fall begun in late trade on Wednesday to end the day down 37.72 points, or 1.17 percent, at 3,196.03 points. Declines had set in late the previous day after a wave of selling on U.S. markets.

A weak opening on the Dow Jones Industrial Index weighed on the market and jitters ahead of Friday's triple witching options expiry added to volatility, but dealers said the feeling on the market was that prices had been pushed up to unrealistic levels.
"We haven't had really negative numbers but I suppose people are thinking now that it can't get better than this. And we really need to clear the air here," said a Frankfurt dealer.

A larger than expected rise in German January M3 money supply data on Thursday briefly added to pressure on the market, although the effect was shortlived as economists said this would not motivate a German interest rate hike.

Insurer Allianz AG Holding was hit early on, but pared earlier losses to end down 24.20 marks at 3,210.80 points. The insurer was hit by profit-taking after announcing a double digit rise in earnings for 1996, in line with expectations.
Engineering group Mannesmann AG ended unchanged at 676 marks. Earlier it announced a doubling of its telecommunications earnings and said it planned to raise its dividend by one mark.
Although some dealers said the dividend hike was less than had been expected, Mannesmann's overall message was neutral to positive.
Siemens AG ended the day down 13 pfennigs at 84.22 marks, off earlier lows, after a projection that its semi-conductors division would triple sales by the year 2001.
Dealers said the market was pessimistic on the division in general, whose profits fell to 603 million marks in the 1995/1996 business year from 793 million.
Volkswagen AG was one of the few winners on the day, ending up seven marks at 802 marks, lifted by news that a Spanish truckers strike, which had hit its production there, was over.

Sportswear maker Puma AG ended up 4.72 percent at 62.10 marks after it said expected a favourable result in the first quarter of the year and reported higher profits for the first nine months of the year.
